replies.author: ResidentialHooligan
replies.body:
Because the sheer volume of slop that is put out in comparison is a tidal wave. 

Pre AI you’d have some stinker games but they were often not that common. 

Nowadays take a look at any semi popular video game released and you’ll see 10’s of hastily slapped together clones that are released en masse to try and capitalise on the popularity. 

As a consumer I never saw mass copycat clones made in a slop fashion until the AI workflows became popular. 

That’s where my delineation lies between the two.

replies.author: SimplySoda2
replies.body: Before AI, they called it asset flipping.

replies.author: ResidentialHooligan
replies.body:
Totally different thing, asset flips were usually poor recreations or reimaginations. 

These new ones are line for line replications due to the speed at which AI can decompile and clone a game. 

You’re also still ignoring the sheer volume at which this happens now, asset flips were minor compared to most titles.

replies.author: SimplySoda2
replies.body:
Some asset flips were just mashups of premade assets and gameplay systems, sometimes without even having a proper gameplay loop. Others were practically untouched demo scenes from FPS kits or asset-store templates being sold as finished games.

Asset flipping wasn't necessarily about poorly recreating or reimagining another game. Sometimes it was just taking existing assets, templates, and systems, throwing them together, and publishing the result with minimal effort.

I agree AI makes cloning existing games significantly easier and faster, but low-effort copycat games and mass-produced shovelware certainly weren't new concepts.

replies.author: ResidentialHooligan
replies.body:
I’m not saying the concept is new, cloning and slop has been around since the beginning of time. Even artwork back in history had people cloning it lol. 

I think it’s more-so that the volume of it taking place appears to be orders of magnitudes larger than pre LLM assistance which is probably partially why there is so much backlash.

replies.author: VladizT
replies.body: You are conflating two different scenarios: a person who knows how to write code without AI and uses it to achieve a specific goal, versus someone who lacks that knowledge and relies on AI to do everything for them and it is the latter that will soon become ubiquitous. This is why I brought up the example of a junior developer, they typically lack that foundational knowledge and either figure things out on their own or simply have AI do all the work. Consequently, there is a massive gap between a junior who relies on AI and one who has learned to code through their own efforts. A junior who depends on AI might not even know how to craft an effective prompt, precisely because they don’t understand how the code should be written in the first place. Since AI-generated code is being used everywhere, junior developers will inevitably turn to it at every opportunity. While it’s convenient to have AI fix a bug in five seconds, this process deprives your brain of the chance to overcome challenges a crucial part of cognitive development. It can reach an absurd point where you end up calling on AI for even the most trivial tasks, simply because you or rather, your brain are too lazy to do it yourself. If you don’t understand the code, you are forced to rely entirely on AI, which effectively renders you helpless. AI is a trap that will lead to a total degradation in the quality of all code and create complete dependency on AI providers.

replies.author: Dixxi_Normous1080p
replies.body: I completely agree. AI in the hands of competent devs is whats important. But we were initially talking about the MW4 devs using coding agents. And I'm sure they have some excellent devs there who truly know how to make the most of them.

replies.author: VladizT
replies.body: I am certain that the vast majority of MW4 is built upon code written long before the advent of AI, it is not code created from scratch using AI. If someone were to attempt to build something like that from the ground up using AI without simply copying what already exists it would be a disaster. Generally, any games I see that are built entirely using AI end up looking like mere prototypes or carbon copies of existing works. Artists today often claim that code is free and easy, yet they rank even lower than junior developers largely because, to them, code is essentially a black box. It feels as though the actual code is being relegated to the background, while the wrapper the presentation takes center stage. I suspect that AAA companies will be the least affected, as they already possess a solid foundation of high-quality, pre-existing work, even if they do incorporate AI. However, for those attempting to build everything from scratch, it remains highly questionable where such an approach will ultimately lead.
